title: Writing as an Iterative Process: From First Draft to Final Version
brief: Explain the core idea that writing is a process involving multiple drafts rather than a single finished product. Draw on the module's statement that providing students with written feedback on their papers and allowing them to revise their work shows students that writing is a process and may involve writing multiple drafts. Describe how formative feedback shapes changes in subsequent drafts, while summative feedback is applied to final versions, using the module's distinction between these two types of teacher response. Emphasise that students actively engage in writing as an iterative process, as the module illustrates through the example of a student noticing a missing introduction in a peer's essay and then returning to check their own work.

title: Responding to Student Writing Without Overwhelming It
brief: Focus on the challenge of providing feedback without drowning student writing in corrections. Use the module's acknowledgement that the main challenge of providing feedback before assigning a grade is that extra time and effort are required for teachers to provide feedback on drafts and then read and score revised papers. Explain the module's position that teachers should still provide their own corrections and feedback alongside peer input so that students are not relying only on student feedback. Discuss how the teacher in course material provides feedback around the same time as peer review, creating a balanced approach that keeps the teacher's role meaningful without making it the sole source of correction.

title: Correction Codes: Marking the Margin, Not Rewriting the Line
brief: Define a correction code as a small set of marginal symbols that locates and classifies errors without supplying the repair. Introduce practical symbols such as sp, wo, vt, ww, art, agr, p, and the missing-word caret. Explain why the restraint is pedagogically important: a fully corrected draft turns revision into copying, while a coded draft requires the learner to locate, diagnose, and repair the problem. Include selective-marking guidance: prioritize target-language errors, errors that obscure meaning, and recurring patterns rather than coding every slip. Make clear that a code prompts knowledge the writer partly has; it does not replace a needed explanation.

title: Introducing the Code and Reading a Coded Draft
brief: Show how to introduce a correction code gradually, beginning with three or four frequent symbols, modeling each with a sample sentence, and keeping a visible legend. Use a complete worked draft in which Daniel revises verb-tense, agreement, and missing-word problems from marginal codes without the teacher rewriting any line. Explain the diagnostic distinction between a code that the learner repairs successfully, which suggests present but unmonitored knowledge, and a code that remains unrepaired, which signals a gap requiring teaching. Place coded feedback explicitly between drafts so it functions formatively.

title: Goals and Learner Autonomy: What Peer Review Achieves
brief: Describe the learning goals of the self-editing and peer feedback activity as listed in the module: students notice their own strengths and feel proud of them; they identify missing or weak information; they compare their writing with peers' work; they develop inner criteria for what makes a strong essay; and they encounter different kinds of writing. Explain how the module connects this activity to learner autonomy, noting that students learn they can rely on each other and themselves, can receive good feedback from peers, and are capable of correcting their own writing. Use the module's point that students with weaker writing skills can notice for themselves what needs to be improved, thereby strengthening their skills and becoming more autonomous writers.

title: Challenges, Benefits, and Adapting Peer Review Across Contexts
brief: Present the module's balanced account of the challenges and benefits of peer feedback as an alternative assessment approach. Challenges include the teacher having less control over what happens and the time required to prepare and set up the activity; benefits include students feeling more in control of their own writing and not seeing the teacher as the only authority. Use the module's guidance on adapting the activity for different proficiency levels: for beginning-level students, simpler topics and single words or symbols such as plus signs, minus signs, question marks, or happy and sad faces; for more advanced students, more complex expectations. Close by drawing on the module's statement that overall, students become better writers and more autonomous learners, and that the benefits outweigh the challenges.
